name: Metal braces

lead: Metal braces are the standard route to straight teeth for teens and adults: steel brackets bonded to the teeth and joined by a wire gradually bring crooked or gapped teeth into a straighter, more even smile.

The wire applies steady pressure and bone remodels around the moved teeth. They are the most common type of braces and are well established in orthodontics. Research has also looked at how laypeople rate the attractiveness of different appliances and what motivates adult patients.

paras: Brackets are bonded in a visit, then adjusted every few weeks. Treatment commonly lasts from about six months to two and a half years, followed by retainers to hold the result. Elastic ties or built-in clips hold the wire.
Plaque build-up and gum inflammation are reported if cleaning slips, along with soreness and some root shortening. Braces are very visible. Retainers afterward are needed to limit relapse.

angle.text: Metal braces are the standard route to straight teeth for teens and adults. Brackets and a wire apply steady pressure, and the teeth move into line over months. Alignment improves gradually through treatment, and the method is well established in orthodontics.

lead: Metal braces are the traditional form of fixed orthodontic appliance: stainless steel brackets bonded to the teeth and joined by an archwire, held with elastic ties or built-in clips (self-ligating) [1]. They apply steady pressure so that bone remodels around moved teeth, and are the most common type of braces [1].

Treatment usually lasts from about six months to two and a half years, followed by retainers [1]. Research on how others perceive appliances includes laypeople's ratings of attractiveness, acceptability and value of different appliances [2], and surveys of adult orthodontic patients' motivations [3].

paras: Stainless steel brackets are the most common; self-ligating variants use a clip instead of elastic ties and may shorten treatment and reduce discomfort [1]. Gold-plated and titanium versions exist for nickel-sensitive patients [1]. Nickel-titanium wires, developed in 1959 and used for full treatments from 1979, deliver light constant force [1].
Orthodontic devices trace to antiquity, with Pierre Fauchard often credited with founding modern orthodontics in the 1700s and Edward Angle classifying malocclusion in the 1900s [1].

Metal braces are highly visible, which motivates clear, ceramic and lingual alternatives [1]. A 2009 study had 50 adults rate photographs of appliances on attractiveness, acceptability and value [2]. A Saudi cross-sectional study examined the effect of appliance type on hiring prospects [4]. A survey of 276 adult patients examined motivation and daily-life effects [3].

Plaque accumulation around braces can cause gingivitis, and poor hygiene may lead to gum disease or recession; soreness after adjustments and some root shortening are common [1]. In vitro work has compared microbial adhesion across bracket and wire types [5].
No trial of metal braces as a looksmaxxing intervention was found. Observational and survey research on perceptions of appliances exists [2][3][4], and in vitro microbial adhesion work [5].

timeline.event: Nitinol alloy developed; used for full treatments from 1979.[1]
